job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Esther Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Esther, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at six for prayer, then I help get my two little brothers off to school, since Mum starts early at the care home. We rent a house in Handsworth, in Birmingham, and I share a room with my brother Daniel, who's twelve. I studied computer science, top of my year, with internships at a bank's IT team and at a logistics software firm. Mornings I apply for jobs, and afternoons I build a booking app for a hair salon on my street. Five months out, fifty applications, four interviews, no offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, praise God, because that gives people time. But I'd add that nobody should relax, since AI is already a good assistant for those who use it. I use it every day to write code and test it, and it makes me about twice as fast on small things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a plateau is not the problem. The problem is that banks and big firms stopped hiring graduates for a while, and the few openings go to people from a handful of universities. I owe thirty-two thousand pounds, and my mum can't help with that, because she barely covers rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the salon app until it earns. Then I'd go to the barbers, the African grocery and the nail bars on my street and offer the same. I'd charge twenty pounds a month, which is cheap enough for them and adds up for me. I'd also keep applying to ten jobs a week, and I'd ask my pastor to introduce me to a couple of businessmen from the church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fired up, honestly. A bit tired too, but I'd rather be building than sitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the openings go to a handful of universities. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Annoying, because my degree is as good as theirs and my marks are better. But I don't want to sound bitter. I'd rather prove it by building something people pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your mum say about the app idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She says, my daughter, don't forget your real job, which means a salaried one. But she also took in sewing for years, so she understands working for yourself. She gave me her sewing table for a desk.

say: A plateau gives people **time**, but nobody should relax, since AI is already a good assistant.
I use it **every day**, and it makes me twice as fast.
think: The problem is that big firms stopped hiring graduates, and openings go to **a handful of universities**.
With thirty-two thousand pounds owed, I can't count on **Mum's help**.
do: Push the **salon app** until it earns, then sell it to barbers and grocers.
Charge **twenty pounds a month** and keep applying to ten jobs weekly.
Ask my **pastor** to introduce me to church businessmen.
feel: **Fired up** and a bit tired, preferring to build than to sit.
S0.quote: I'd rather prove it by building something people pay for.
fieldNote: Frames her **drive** through faith and family, not bitterness.
Uses her mum's **sewing table** as a desk, a small symbol of self-employment.
Debt and **thin family money** keep her mood anxious despite her energy.

steps.text: Sign up the hair salon and sell the booking app to neighbouring shops
Apply to ten graduate jobs every week
Use AI daily to write and test code twice as fast
Ask the pastor to introduce me to businessmen at church

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the right kind of change for people who work hard and keep learning. Companies that use these tools will need fewer people, so the answer is to start something yourself or to learn to run the tools. I'd say it at church and on my channel, where I show how I build things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think banks and big firms will hire fewer juniors, and that's the door I was aiming at. In my internship at the bank, the test checking I did is the sort of task the card lists. But I also think small businesses will want help with the tools and don't know how, and that's where I can work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the app idea into a small service: set up booking, messages and invoices for small shops using AI tools, and charge a monthly fee. I'd aim for ten paying customers by summer. I'd keep applying to firms that build with AI, since they need people who already use it. And I'd put money into a laptop with a better chip, since mine is old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and anxious at once. It's like a door shutting and a window opening, and I'm trying to climb through the window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your channel, and why do you run it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a small video channel where I show how I build the app, step by step, with about four hundred followers. It's my portfolio and, hopefully, a way to find customers. I also like teaching, and my brothers watch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the ten customers don't come by summer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I take a job, any job, including support or testing, and keep the business on weekends. I'd never leave my family without income, so I'd rather have a small paycheque and a small business than a big idea alone.

say: It's the right kind of change for people who work hard and **keep learning**.
The answer is to **start something** or learn to run the tools.
think: Banks and big firms will hire **fewer juniors**, and that was my target door.
**Small businesses** need help with the tools, and I can give it.
do: Turn the app into a **monthly service** for small shops and aim for ten customers by summer.
Apply to firms that **build with AI**.
Buy a **better laptop** for the work.
feel: **Excited and anxious**, like climbing through a window as a door shuts.
S1.quote: I'd rather have a small paycheque and a small business than a big idea alone.
fieldNote: Her **video channel** doubles as portfolio, marketing and teaching.
Sets a **summer deadline** for ten customers.
Admits a fallback job, because **family income** comes before pride.

steps.text: Sell a booking and invoicing service to ten small shops by summer
Post weekly videos showing how I build with AI tools
Apply to firms that build products with AI
Buy a faster laptop for client work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that this is a time for faith and sense. I'd tell people to look after their families, save what they can, and help their neighbours. I'd say the government should keep order and support the vulnerable, but that those of us who can work should be given a way to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm frightened, but I don't think I'm paralysed. My business idea sells to the exact people who will be pushed hardest, small shops, and AGI will build a better booking app than mine in a month. I owe thirty-two thousand and it won't wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a paid job within six months, any job, even call centre or care work with my mum's company. I'd keep the small business for the shops I already have, and not expect it to grow. I'd pay the loan minimum, and give to the church even if it's small, because I believe in that. I'd also teach my brothers how to use the tools while they're still at school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and steady, at the same time. My faith holds me up, but my hands still shake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AGI would build a better booking app within a month. What does that do to your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the app is a bridge, not a destination. I'd use it to get cash for a year, and then let it go. I'd rather know now than build a castle on sand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does two years change what you teach your brothers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd teach them to be useful to people in person, to be good with tools, and to keep praying. Daniel's twelve and wants to design games, and I'd say, do it, but learn how to fix things with your hands as well.

say: This is a time for **faith and sense**: look after families, save and help neighbours.
Government should **support the vulnerable** but also give workers a way to work.
think: AGI will build a better booking app than mine in **a month**.
I'm frightened but **not paralysed**, and the loan won't wait.
do: Get a **paid job** within six months, even call centre or care work.
Keep the **shop customers** but don't expect growth.
Teach my **brothers** the tools while they're in school.
feel: **Scared and steady**: faith holds her up but her hands still shake.
S2.quote: I'd rather know now than build a castle on sand.
fieldNote: Her **business** itself is exposed, which she admits calmly.
Thinks about her **brothers'** futures at the same time as her own.

steps.text: Take any paid job, such as call centre or care work, within six months
Keep the existing shop customers on the booking app for cash
Pay only the loan minimum and hold the rest in savings
Teach my brothers to use AI tools and fix things by hand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's enough time for people who prepare, and I'd tell them to start today. Learn the tools, learn a trade, build something, and save. I'd also say that work gives dignity and that people should be given a way to work for it, not just handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel hopeful. A first job within the year is likely, and with the tools I'd rise quickly. Then I'd have three years before robots arrive to build savings and a second income. The loan would shrink a lot, and I'd be more careful with money than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first good job, probably at a software firm, and keep the small business on the side. I'd spend a year learning a hands-on skill alongside, like networking hardware or smart-building systems, which robots will take longest to replace. I'd save a quarter of my pay. And I'd help my mum move out of the care home job into something less tiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful and busy. It feels like a marathon that I have time to train for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you move your mum out of the care home job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's on her feet twelve hours and her knees are going. She won't say it, but I see it. I'd like to get her into a role like scheduling or admin at the same home, which she'd do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you build with the side business over five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small software company with one or two employees from my church or street. I'd like to give people a first job, since I know how hard that is. It's a small dream and I'm not shy about it.

say: Five years is **enough time** for people who prepare: learn the tools, learn a trade, save.
Work gives **dignity**, and people should be given a way to work.
think: A **first job** within a year is likely, and the tools help me rise quickly.
Three years before robots lets me build **savings** and a second **income**.
do: Take the first good **software job** and keep the small business going.
Learn **smart-building systems** or networking hardware, which last longer.
Save **a quarter** of my pay and help my mum change jobs.
feel: **Hopeful and busy**, like training for a marathon.
S3.quote: I'd like to give people a first job, since I know how hard that is.
fieldNote: Builds a **hands-on second skill** to ride the robot delay.
Includes her **mum's** health and knees in the plan.
Her mood is **uneasy** because her adaptability and side business give her control.

steps.text: Take the first good software job and keep the side business
Learn smart-building systems alongside the job
Save a quarter of each paycheque
Help Mum move from care work into admin at the home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, thank God for ten years. I'd tell people it's enough time to do something real: start a business, learn a skill, build a family. And I'd say that governments should make it easy for people to try, not hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine, probably more than fine. I'd have a job, a business and a plan, and I'd have cleared the loan. The danger is that people feel there's no hurry and then they're caught out. I won't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with a good job and use the first three years to save and build the business. I'd hire one person from my church for the business, maybe two. I'd take a part-time master's if my employer pays for it. And I'd help Daniel and my other brother, Joel, into university without debt, by saving a little each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. A proper deep breath for the first time since graduation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to do differently from how people handled your degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my brothers to study with a plan, with work experience and no huge loan. I'd tell my brothers to pick what pays, then do what they love on the side. I wish someone had told me that at seventeen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with the two-year picture, what changes in your first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job for the learning and for the chance to grow. I wouldn't treat the app as a lifeboat. And I'd sleep better, which matters more than it sounds.

say: Ten years is **enough time** to do something real: a business, a skill, a family.
Governments should make it **easy to try**, not hard.
think: I'd be **fine, probably more**: a job, a business and the loan cleared.
The danger is people feeling there's **no hurry**, then getting caught out.
do: Start with a good job and use **three years** to save and build the business.
Hire **one or two people** from church and study part-time on employer money.
Save monthly so my brothers can go to **university without debt**.
feel: **Good**: a proper deep breath for the first time since graduating.
S4.quote: I'd tell my brothers to pick what pays, then do what they love on the side.
fieldNote: Plans to **hire** from her church, giving others a first job.
Wants her **brothers** to avoid her debt.
Sleep appears again as a **mood marker**, as in other scenarios.

steps.text: Take a good job and spend three years learning and saving
Grow the booking business and hire one person from church
Clear the student loan within about eight years
Save monthly so my brothers can study without debt

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits my business plan and my first job together, and my mum can't carry me. What would help is quick access to a first paid job, like a graduate placement, and a slower loan schedule. Also a business grant for small sellers, so people can start without risking everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not looking for a handout. I want a door to open so I can work, pay my debts and look after my family. Faith and hard work are my plan, and I'd like a chance to show it.

headlineQuote: I'm not looking for a handout. I want a door to open so I can work
portrait: Esther is a **top computer science** graduate in Birmingham, five months without an offer.
She lives with her mother and two brothers in a rented house, owes **thirty-two thousand pounds**, and prays each morning.
She uses **AI every day**, builds a booking app for neighbourhood shops and runs a small video channel.
She is **traditional and entrepreneurial**: free markets, work over handouts, church and family first.
Her mood is **anxious** through two years and eases to uneasy with five or ten years of warning.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it hits her **business plan** and first job together.
whatWouldHelp: A **graduate placement** for a first paid job and a slower loan schedule.
A **business grant** for small sellers so people can start without risking everything.
